meta.label: Notes
meta.attribution: Built from providers' own security, privacy and help documentation, terms of service, pricing pages and published source repositories, not measured data. Plans, prices and features change often, so check the current pages before relying on any of these. Prices are US list prices unless a currency is stated. Privacy reflects whether the company that stores or syncs the notes can read them: local-only storage and end-to-end encryption score high, server-side encryption where the provider holds the keys scores low, and an encryption claim that no independent analysis was read for is scored below one with such analysis, with the cell saying which case applies. Openness reflects whether client and server code is published and under what licence; a source-available licence that limits use is scored below an open-source licence. Portability reflects whether notes leave in open formats such as Markdown, HTML or plain text and how complete the export is. Respect reflects whether the business model runs on advertising or on selling subscriptions and software. Accessibility covers how easy a tool is to start and to sync across a person's devices and share from; it does not measure access for disabled users. Economical reflects the free allowance and the price of the paid tier that unlocks syncing where one exists. No official register of note-taking apps was found, so the record here is the providers' own legal and technical documents and their public source repositories. Compared here are apps whose main job is keeping notes. Task managers, office suites, team wikis such as Outline, reference managers such as Zotero, and email-based tools do a different job and are not compared. Simplenote is not compared because its site refused automated requests. Evernote's help centre refused them too, so Evernote's export cell rests on Joplin's documentation of importing ENEX files. Notion's terms and privacy policy load only inside its app and could not be read, so its openness cell is empty. Google Keep's economical cell is empty because no page that could be read states its price, and OneNote's rests on the title of its web page. Suggest changes via Contribute.

criteria.label: Stored so the provider cannot read notes
Easy to start, sync across devices and share

products.name: Apple Notes

privacy.note: Apple's iCloud data security table lists Notes as encrypted in transit and on the server with the keys stored by Apple under standard protection, and as end-to-end encrypted with keys on trusted devices only when the optional Advanced Data Protection setting is on.

openness.note: Apple's iCloud terms say Apple and its licensors own the service and its software, which contain proprietary and confidential information that may be used only to use the service under the agreement.

portability.note: Apple's Notes guide for Mac says notes can be exported as PDF or Markdown files or copied as Markdown, and that Markdown, TXT, RTF, RTFD, HTML and Evernote ENEX files can be imported.

respect.note: Apple's privacy policy says ads from its advertising platform may appear in the App Store, Apple News, Stocks and the Apple TV app, none of which is Notes, and says that platform does not link data from Apple's apps with third-party data for targeted advertising.

accessibility.note: Apple's requirements page says Notes with upgraded iCloud features is available on iPhone, iPad and Mac, and that only some Android devices can use iCloud.com, which works best in browsers on macOS, iOS, iPadOS and Windows.

economical.note: Apple's iCloud+ page gives 5 GB of iCloud storage free and lists 50 GB at 0.99 US dollars a month; the page lists no separate charge for Notes.

links.label: Secure notes in the Notes app

products.description: The notes app built into iPhone, iPad and Mac, syncing through iCloud. Ordinary notes sit under standard iCloud protection where Apple holds the keys, and a note locked with a passphrase is end-to-end encrypted.

products.name: Google Keep

privacy.note: Google's privacy policy says it collects the content people create and upload and that automated systems analyze content to provide features and to detect abuse such as spam, malware and illegal content; the policy names no user-held key option.

openness.note: Google's terms of service prohibit reverse engineering its services or the underlying technology to extract trade secrets or other proprietary information, except as applicable law allows, so Keep is offered as a proprietary service.

portability.note: Google's Keep help page says a person can export and download Keep data that has not been deleted, as an archive to keep or to use in another service, and lists the download as note text and list items, attachments, colour, pinned and archived state, collaborators and the label list; it names no file format.

respect.note: Google's privacy policy says it does not show personalized ads based on content from Drive, Gmail or Photos, which does not name Keep, and also says automated systems analyze content to provide personalized ads and other features.

accessibility.note: Google's Keep help says a person can create, edit and share notes with Keep and walks through installing the Android app; Keep is used with a Google Account.

products.description: Google's quick notes and lists app, tied to a Google account. Google's privacy policy names Drive, Gmail and Photos when it says content is not used for personalized ads, and does not name Keep.

products.name: Microsoft OneNote

privacy.note: Microsoft's OneNote help says a section can be protected with a password, that if the password is forgotten not even Microsoft Technical Support could unlock the notes, and that audio and video recordings cannot be password-protected.

openness.note: Microsoft's Services Agreement says the software is licensed, not sold, and that a person may not disassemble, decompile, decrypt, hack, emulate, exploit or reverse engineer any software or other aspect of the services, except as applicable copyright law expressly permits.

portability.note: Microsoft's help page says a copy of a notebook can be downloaded or imported through OneNote for the web only, that it works only for notebooks on personal OneDrive accounts and not for work or school OneDrive or SharePoint, and that the export arrives as a Zip file.

respect.note: Microsoft's privacy statement says it does not use personal files, photos or documents to target ads, and also says it uses data for advertising on Microsoft and third-party properties, which a person can opt out of.

accessibility.note: Microsoft's OneNote page describes notes accessible across all devices, with a mobile app for iOS or Android and a sign-in for the web version.

economical.note: Microsoft's OneNote for the web page is titled Take notes anywhere for free.

products.description: Microsoft's notebook app, free to use and stored in OneDrive. A section can be locked with a password, and Microsoft documents downloading a whole notebook only through OneNote for the web, for notebooks on a personal OneDrive.

products.name: Evernote

privacy.note: Evernote says everything put into Evernote is private by default and that its systems automatically analyze data to power features such as search and related notes, while never giving or selling content to a third party for advertising.

openness.note: Evernote's terms say a person agrees not to modify, create derivative works of, decompile or otherwise attempt to extract source code from any Evernote software, unless an open source license or written permission allows it.

portability.note: Joplin's documentation says complete Evernote notebooks, notes, tags, attachments and metadata can be imported from ENEX files, though recognition data is not preserved and, for very complex notes, colours, font sizes and font faces are not imported.

respect.note: Evernote says it is not a big data company and does not try to make money from note content, and that it never gives or sells content to a third party for advertising; the site footer names Bending Spoons US Inc. as the owner.

accessibility.note: Evernote's plan comparison lists the free plan at 50 notes, 1 GB of storage and sync on 1 device, the Starter plan at 1,000 notes on 3 devices, and the Advanced plan with unlimited notes and devices.

economical.note: Evernote's plan comparison limits the free plan to 50 notes, 20 tags and 1 device; it does not show paid prices, so the cost of lifting those limits is not quoted here.

products.description: The long-standing notes service, now run by Bending Spoons. Its free plan is capped at 50 notes on one device, and its systems read note content to power search and related notes.

products.name: Notion

privacy.note: Notion's security page says customer data is encrypted at rest using AES-256 and in transit using TLS 1.2 or greater, and describes no end-to-end or user-held-key option.

portability.note: Notion's help page says a page, database or entire workspace can be exported at any time as PDF, CSV or HTML, and as Markdown and CSV, where a database exports as CSV with Markdown files for subpages.

respect.note: Notion's pricing page sells Free, Plus, Business and Enterprise plans, with Plus at 10 US dollars per member a month, so the business runs on subscriptions; the page also lists trial AI features in the free plan.

accessibility.note: Notion's pricing page describes the free plan as for individuals organizing personal projects, with databases, basic forms and sites, and Notion Calendar included.

economical.note: Notion's pricing page lists the Free plan at 0 US dollars per member a month and Plus at 10 US dollars per member a month.

products.description: A notes and database workspace with a free plan for individuals. Data is encrypted at rest and in transit, and Notion describes no end-to-end option.

products.name: Bear

privacy.note: Bear says it syncs notes through Apple's CloudKit, that everything stored there is encrypted with Apple's private keys, and that Shiny Frog does not want to access the data at all.

openness.note: Bear's terms say the service and its original content, features and functionality are and will remain the exclusive property of Shiny Frog Ltd. and its licensors.

portability.note: Bear's export page says the free version exports notes as .txt, .md, .textbundle, .bearnote and .rtf, and Bear Pro adds HTML, DOCX, PDF and JPG.

respect.note: Bear says it does not want to sell personal information and does not want to access user data at all, which it gives as the reason it relies on Apple's CloudKit to sync.

accessibility.note: Bear's home page lists Mac, iPhone and iPad as the platforms it runs on.

economical.note: Bear's Pro page lists a monthly subscription at 2.99 US dollars or a yearly one at 29.99 dollars, both with a 7-day free trial, and says Pro unlocks iCloud sync across devices.

products.description: A Markdown notes app for Mac, iPhone and iPad that syncs through Apple's CloudKit. iCloud sync and per-note encryption are part of the Bear Pro subscription.

products.name: Obsidian

privacy.note: Obsidian's privacy page says the desktop and mobile apps save all data locally on the device and never send it to Obsidian's servers, collect no telemetry, and end-to-end encrypt Obsidian Sync data including file names.

openness.note: Obsidian's license overview says Obsidian owns and reserves rights to the code in the app, which is protected by copyright, while its GitHub organisation publishes the plugin API, importer and web clipper under MIT.

portability.note: Obsidian's help says notes are stored as Markdown-formatted plain text files in a vault, which is a folder on the local file system, so other text editors and file managers can open them.

respect.note: Obsidian's about page says it is 100% supported by its users, not investors, and its pricing page sells optional Sync and Publish add-ons.

accessibility.note: Obsidian's pricing page says the app is free with no sign-up, and that syncing notes across devices is an optional paid Sync add-on with end-to-end encryption and version history.

economical.note: Obsidian's pricing page lists the app as free without limits, Sync at 4 US dollars a month billed annually or 5 billed monthly, and Publish at 8 dollars a month billed annually.

products.description: A notes app that keeps notes as Markdown files in a folder on the device, free for all uses. The app itself is proprietary; encrypted sync is a paid add-on.

products.name: Joplin

privacy.note: Joplin's documentation says end-to-end encryption is supported on all applications and keeps notes readable only by their owner, and that it has to be enabled manually on one device first and then synced to the others.

openness.note: Joplin's licence file says all code in the repository is AGPL-3.0-or-later unless a directory contains its own licence file, and names the server directory as one that has its own licence file.

portability.note: Joplin's documentation says it exports to the lossless JEX format, to a raw directory format with one file per item, and to HTML and PDF, and imports Evernote ENEX, Markdown files and OneNote exports.

respect.note: Joplin's plans page sells Joplin Cloud from 2.99 euros a month, and its site says the app is open source and that Joplin Cloud is based in France.

accessibility.note: Joplin's site lists apps for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS plus a terminal app, syncing through Joplin Cloud, Dropbox, OneDrive and other services that a person sets up.

economical.note: Joplin's plans page lists Joplin Cloud Basic at 2.99 euros a month or 2.40 euros billed yearly with 2 GB, and Pro at 5.99 euros a month; the apps themselves are downloaded from the site.

products.description: An open-source notes app for desktop, phone and terminal, syncing through Joplin Cloud, Dropbox, OneDrive and other services. End-to-end encryption is available on all apps but has to be switched on.

products.name: Standard Notes

privacy.note: Standard Notes says it protects notes and files with audited end-to-end encryption and that only the user has the keys needed to decrypt the data; this rests on the app's own statement and no independent analysis was read for this entry.

openness.note: Standard Notes' GitHub organisation publishes the app under AGPL-3.0 and a server described as fully self-hostable under GPL-3.0.

portability.note: Standard Notes' help page says backup files are plain text and can be downloaded encrypted or decrypted, with the decrypted zip holding a restorable backup file and a folder with each note as its own plain text file.

respect.note: Standard Notes' plans page offers a free plan with end-to-end encryption and unlimited device sync and sells Productivity at 90 US dollars a year and Professional at 120 dollars a year.

accessibility.note: Standard Notes' plans page lists unlimited device sync on web, desktop and mobile in the free plan, with the full editing experience unlocked by the paid Productivity plan.

economical.note: Standard Notes' plans page lists a free plan, Productivity at 90 US dollars a year and Professional at 120 dollars a year.

products.description: An end-to-end encrypted notes app whose apps and self-hostable server are published on GitHub. It joined Proton in 2024 and keeps its own paid plans.

products.name: Notesnook

privacy.note: Notesnook's privacy policy says data is encrypted on the device with XChaCha20-Poly1305 and Argon2 before transmission and that the company does not sell, collect, use, read or modify what users create; this rests on Notesnook's own statement and no independent analysis was read for this entry.

openness.note: Notesnook's GitHub organisation publishes the app under GPL-3.0 and the sync server under AGPL-3.0, which it describes as in alpha for self-hosting.

portability.note: Notesnook's help page says notes can be exported as PDF, HTML, Markdown, Markdown with frontmatter and plain text on all apps, and that multi-note exports on desktop and web arrive as a zip.

respect.note: Notesnook's privacy policy is issued by Streetwriters (Private) Limited, which honors Do Not Track and says it does not use advertising when that signal is on; the pricing page sells paid plans.

accessibility.note: Notesnook's pricing page lists downloads for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS and the web, and unlimited notes on every device in the free plan.

economical.note: Notesnook's pricing page lists a free plan with unlimited notes and 50 MB of storage a month, Essential at 19.99 US dollars a year and Pro at 69.99 dollars a year.

products.description: An end-to-end encrypted notes app with apps and sync server published under open licences and a free plan with unlimited notes. It keeps its servers in Germany.

products.name: Logseq

privacy.note: Logseq's database-version documentation says desktop graphs live in a local graph directory with automatic backups in a backups folder, and that its paid, invite-only Sync asks the user to set an encryption password.

openness.note: The Logseq repository on GitHub is licensed under AGPL-3.0, and its documentation says the invite-only Sync can also be self-hosted.

portability.note: Logseq's database-version documentation says a graph can be exported as a SQLite file, as a zip with assets, as standard Markdown without block properties, which cannot capture all data, or as EDN, and that a Markdown graph can be imported.

respect.note: Logseq's README asks users to support its contributors through Open Collective, and its database-version documentation describes Sync as a paid feature that is currently invite only.

accessibility.note: Logseq's README says the database version is in beta with a new mobile app and real-time sync in alpha, that data loss is possible, and recommends backups.

economical.note: Logseq's README offers the app for download and points to Open Collective for donations, and the database-version documentation lists Sync as its paid feature.

products.description: An open-source outliner for linked notes. Its new database version stores a graph in a SQLite database and is in beta, and the README warns that data loss is possible.

products.name: Anytype

privacy.note: Anytype's documentation says a person's key is generated on the device and never sent to Anytype's servers, and that not even Anytype can see the content of a space; this rests on Anytype's own statement and no independent analysis was read for this entry.

openness.note: Anytype's repository is under the Any Source Available License 1.0, which lets a licensee use, modify and redistribute the software only for non-commercial use, or for commercial use in allowed networks.

portability.note: Anytype's documentation says a channel can be exported as Markdown or Any-Block, and objects as PDF or HTML, with JSON or Protobuf file formats, on desktop only.

respect.note: Anytype says it is made by Any, a Swiss association, and its pricing page sells paid memberships from 4 US dollars a month.

accessibility.note: Anytype's home page describes an offline-first vault on the device with native iOS and Android apps, and the pricing page lists a free plan with 100 MB of remote storage and 10 shared channels.

economical.note: Anytype's pricing page lists a free plan with 100 MB of remote storage, Plus at 4 US dollars a month for 1 GB, Pro at 8 dollars for 10 GB and Ultra at 16 dollars for 100 GB.

products.description: A local-first workspace from a Swiss association, with keys generated on the device and peer-to-peer sync on local networks. Its code is source-available for non-commercial use, and the free plan has 100 MB of remote storage.

products.name: Trilium Notes

privacy.note: Trilium's documentation says protected notes encrypt the title and body with a key protected by the user's password, while note structure, metadata and attributes are not encrypted.

openness.note: The TriliumNext repository on GitHub is licensed under AGPL-3.0, and its README calls Trilium Notes a free and open-source application.

portability.note: Trilium's README lists Evernote import and Markdown import and export, and says the original developer handed the repository to a community project.

respect.note: Trilium's README describes a free and open-source community project, shows GitHub Sponsors and Liberapay patron badges, and says the original developer gave the repository to that community.

accessibility.note: Trilium's README says synchronization uses a self-hosted sync server, with third-party services for hosting one, and lists a touch-optimized mobile frontend rather than a mobile app.

economical.note: Trilium's README describes the application as free and open-source; running a sync server is left to the user or a third-party host.

products.description: A free, open-source notes application built around a tree of notes, with desktop apps and an optional self-hosted sync server. Encryption is a per-note choice, and phones and tablets use a touch-optimized mobile frontend.
